title: ControlFusion: A Controllable Image Fusion Network with Language-Vision De

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3 (Physics-driven Degraded Imaging Model) vs. Section 5.1 (Implementation and Experimental Configurations)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: In Section 3 the RoadScene dataset is cited as '[36]' ('We selected 2,050 high-quality clear images from RoadScene [36], LLVIP [7], and MSRS [29] datasets'), where reference [36] is actually Xu et al.'s 'U2Fusion'. In Section 5.1, the same RoadScene dataset is instead cited as '[35]' ('RoadScene [35]'), where [35] is Xu et al.'s 'FusionDN'. The paper cites two different references for the same dataset inconsistently.

The text states 'd(x) refers to the scene depth, estimated by DepthAnything-V2 [40]', but reference [40] in the bibliography is 'Syed Waqas Zamir, Aditya Arora, Salman Khan, Munawar Hayat, Fahad Shahbaz Khan, and Ming-Hsuan Yang. Restormer: Efficient transformer for high-resolution image restoration', which is unrelated to depth estimation or DepthAnything-V2. This is a clear misattribution/fabricated citation.

The text states 'using the retrained YOLOv8 [26]', but reference [26] is 'Joseph Redmon, Santosh Divvala, Ross Girshick, and Ali Farhadi. You only look once: Unified, real-time object detection', which is the original YOLOv1 paper (2016), not YOLOv8. YOLOv8 has no corresponding peer-reviewed citation matching [26].

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5.2, 'Comparison with Pre-enhancement' paragraph vs. Table 2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims 'ControlFusion achieves superior CLIP-IQA, MUSIQ, and TReS scores across most degradation scenarios.' However, checking Table 2's CLIP-IQA column across the 12 reported scenarios, ControlFusion is NOT the best in 6 of 12 scenarios (VI Low-light: Text-DiFuse 0.192 > 0.183; IR Low-contrast: DRMF 0.208 > 0.196; IR Random noise: Text-DiFuse 0.203 > 0.189; IR Stripe noise: DDFM 0.209 > 0.200; VI(RH)+IR(RN): Text-DiFuse 0.181 > 0.179; VI(LL)+IR(SN): DDFM 0.189 > 0.167). This means ControlFusion is best in only half the scenarios for CLIP-IQA, contradicting the claim of superiority 'across most degradation scenarios'.

The paper explicitly admits: 'our approach uniquely includes pre-enhancement by several SOTA image restoration algorithms tailored to each degradation type. Competing fusion methods are evaluated on raw degraded inputs without pre-enhancement steps, introducing an imbalance that favors our results. A unified baseline applying pre-enhancement across all methods is not provided.' Despite this acknowledged confound, the subsequent conclusions in Table 2 and the surrounding text ('ControlFusion achieves superior ... across most degradation scenarios') are presented as evidence of the model's intrinsic superiority, which is methodologically unsound given the admitted unfair comparison.

The text states 'Liu et al. [17] developed corresponding solutions for ... noise interference', but reference [17] is 'PAIF: Perception-aware infrared-visible image fusion for attack-tolerant semantic segmentation', which addresses adversarial-attack robustness for segmentation rather than generic sensor noise interference, making this attribution misleading.

Both Eq. (2) and Eq. (3) are labeled as computing the same sensor-distortion operator P_s (D_ir^s = P_s(I_ir) in Eq. 2, and D_m^s = P_s(I_m) in Eq. 3), yet they define entirely different and non-equivalent mathematical formulas (contrast/stripe-noise vs. Gaussian-noise/motion-blur). The overall imaging model in Eq. (1) applies a single P_s operator sequentially, but the paper never clarifies how these two inconsistent definitions of P_s combine or are chosen for composite degradation generation, creating an internally inconsistent model description.
